title: Drought response of Eucalyptus species in a common garden experiment: insights from tree rings and wood anatomy
content:
Abstract
Eucalyptus plantations are rapidly expanding across Mediterranean North Africa. Yet, their growth rhythms and wood-anatomical responses to drought remain poorly explored. Revealing these hidden features could redefine reforestation strategies, paving the way for sustainable, climate-adaptive forests for the future. Accordingly, this study evaluated eight juvenile Eucalyptus species (Eucalyptus gomphocephala, Eucalyptus microtheca, Eucalyptus occidentalis, Eucalyptus camaldulensis, Eucalyptus torquata, Eucalyptus diversifolia, Eucalyptus torwood, and Eucalyptus sargentii) grown in a common garden setting under arid Mediterranean conditions in southern Tunisia. Our primary objectives were to quantify the impact of prolonged water deficit and site aridity on radial growth and drought resistance, as well as to assess functional adjustments in xylem anatomical traits. Radial growth was assessed through tree-ring width and basal area increment analyses, while indices like short-term resistance, within-drought habituation, and long-term response were capturing tree performance over consecutive years of drought. Key xylem traits including hydraulic diameter, theoretical hydraulic conductivity, vessel density, and vessel size were measured and analyzed for intercorrelations. Despite their juvenile stage, significant interspecific differences were observed, indicating species-specific responses to water stress. Drought conditions generally resulted in reduced ring widths across most species; however, all exhibited notable short-term wood resistance and intra-drought habituation. Species including E. camaldulensis, E. torquata, E. occidentalis, E. sargentii, and E. torwood exhibited a highly sustained long-term acclimation response. Hydraulic traits were closely linked to combined effects of climatic variability. Additionally, under prolonged water stress, all species showed consistent anatomical adaptations including narrower rings, increased vessel density, and reduced vessel sizes, reflecting a shift toward hydraulic safety mechanisms over transport efficiency. These findings highlight the importance of xylem anatomical plasticity and growth dynamics in enabling drought tolerance in Eucalyptus species, providing valuable insights for selecting suitable species in reforestation and afforestation initiatives within water-limited environments.
